In the Ivankovic case, which is 65 ter 2215 [as interpreted] on page 6, you spoke about the existence of the Council for National Defence, which was sometimes also referred to as the Crisis Staff, but you also confirmed that the counsel for national defence was a permanent body whose members -- were its members ex officio; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Council for National Defence before the war was provided for by the law. Every municipality in the former SFRY had it. At the same time there was a committee on civilian protection and self-defence which was under the dominant influence of the League Communists and social and political organisations. After the first multi-elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Knezevo, that committee lost its influence and importance and it was abolished, and what we mind was the Council for National Defence which continued to function. Since in Knezevo we did not experience any crisis or inter-ethnic conflicts there, there was no power struggle. When the war broke out, as far as I knew we did not have an officially established Crisis Staff. I don't know if people called the Council for National Defence a Crisis Staff. Maybe it was fashionable because that's what happened in other -- in other areas. In my view, it was the Council for National Defence that continued to work throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in your municipality there was no reason for fear or concern among the Muslim population; however, the vicinity of the front line, the events in Travnik, Vecici, and Jajce, and in the neighbouring municipalities did cause some concern, that they communicated with us, and that they asked you to allow them to leave?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I would put it this way: Fear, concern were present among everybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the population of Knezevo, and certainly there was fear and concern among the Muslim population, and you put it very well the reason for all fear and concern was not just one. There were several reasons for fear and concern. One of them was the general situation. A war broke out in the neighbouring municipality of -- of Jajce and Kotor Varos and along the border between the municipalities of Knezevo and Travnik. Muslims were a minority, a huge minority, and from my point of view I would say that they subjectively feelled -- felt fear and concern. How justified that was and whether that fear and concern were justified, I'm sure that they could not think that the official authorities in Knezevo municipality would do them harm. It was just the matter of war and war-related developments that must have caused fear and concern among the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The passing of soldiers, their return from the front line, was that also an element that was feared by both Serbs and Muslims? I'm talking about transit of armed people through your town.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the elements, and as well as the arrival of various paramilitary units and both Serbs and Muslims feared them. Muslims more than the rest of the population, certainly. And, you know, war is an illness in society according to a definition. There were a lot of renegade -- renegades, looters, some old debts surfaced, and all of that resulted in fear and concern among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, on pages 14128 to 14130, you stated that in the course of 1992, one killing happened in late 1991, and there were five or six killings or murders in 1992. Of the victims, five were Muslims, one was Croat, and one was a Serb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you had a lot of problems because you had very few policemen? And let me add that sometimes you had to place your policemen under the command of units in the area when there were attacks.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in your public security station there were Muslim employees as well?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Up until some date in April 1992, Muslims and Croats worked there. They refused to sign that solemn declaration that was sent to us from the security centre in Banja Luka. Croats withdrew to their own territory. They did not come to work on the following day, whereas the Muslim employees quite fairly and correctly asked me to leave and go to Travnik properly; that is to say, with weapons, vehicles, et cetera, to see that if it suits them, they could join the police in Travnik, and if not, they'd go back. I allowed them to do that. They returned on the next day. They were all beaten up. Their clothes were torn. They told me that members of the HVO had attacked them, disarmed them, beaten them up, and then they asked me whether they could go to Jajce the same way with these vehicles, weapons, et cetera. I allowed them to do that, and they went to Jajce and did not return. One lady who's an ethnic Muslim stayed on at the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Croats set up their own station in that concentration that has now become their municipality? Did they go there, or did they go to Jajce?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. Both are plausible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4543. Could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is your report. This was in February. This is a report about the work, who worked for you, and members of the reserve force, and you report that they worked 27 days that month. This is your telegram, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us with this: Number 4, is that Nedzad Krkic? Is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have time now for us to see what the ethnic backgrounds of the others is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? Actually, can we have the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You had a total of 23 policemen, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Approximately, active-duty policemen, and in addition to that there was the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1887, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4544. Could we have a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see here that an order was given to have payments made to these four persons, and is the fourth person on this list Nihada Topal, and is that person of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this has been uploaded, this part, 12589, 65 ter 12589.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're having this checked, let me ask you is it correct -- I saw the oath or rather solemn declarations that were signed by Serbs, too. Is it correct that after the Krajina -- MUP and Krajina were established, the Serbs were also duty-bound to sign a solemn declaration stating that they would act in accordance with the laws and regulations of the ARK Krajina? So it wasn't only the Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. A solemn declaration would be signed, an oath, and I think that also the emblems were changed. Until then there was a five-pointed star, and then that was replaced by a flag which is in force to this day in our part of the world in Republika Srpska. Also, they were different uniforms. Everything was the same for all, and I claim with full responsibility that I signed such an oath as did all the Serbs who worked in my public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in our effort to bring about a reconciliation between the Partisans and Chetniks we opted for a flag rather than a cockade or a five-pointed star or other ideological emblems?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I agree. I think that you are the most deserving person in that respect with all the efforts you made to overcome this rift between the Partisans and Chetniks among the Serb people, and I think that you were quite successful in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you attend any meetings that I attended? I did go to Knezevo -- actually, anywhere. Did you attend any such meetings where I was too?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Not in Knezevo. Two or three times I was in the area of Pale. That was towards the end of 1990. And once in Banja Luka in the beginning of 1991; that is to say, while I was in these political structures of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to say whether you could notice anything extremist in my views or anything that would lead to future conflicts?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing. As such, you were a target, if I can put it that way, of the verbal attacks of these extremist representatives of both the Partisans and Chetniks. That is to say neither of them were satisfied with you. There was this ultra-left extremism and ultra-right extremism, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that my position was to take a soft stance vis-a-vis the other ethnic communities and that nothing should be done that would make then apprehensive in any way?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: While I was a member of these structures and while I attended these meetings, it's not only that you insisted on this soft stance, as you called it, but you also asked us to have full co-operation with the representatives of the other peoples before the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you also insisted on that after the multi-party elections when the power-sharing agreements were being worked out. You said that we should not keep all power in our hands where we were a majority. You said that we should involve the minorities as well, because it was stated that according to this purported agreement with the other two national parties - I never saw this agreement - they would also give Serbs the same kind of opportunities where the Serbs were a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may I just ask you to put once again the other part of your question because I seem to have forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I do anything that would encourage any kind of future conflicts?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No. It was the other way around. Again, I want to say that I'm speaking about the time when I attended various meetings. People were asking you specifically to have Serbs armed because the Croats and the Muslim were is doing that as well. Primarily the Croats were doing that. Then also in Banja Luka there were calls for the Banja Luka Krajina to proclaim some kind of union with the Serb Krajina or those autonomous regions in Croatia. You were absolutely opposed to that, saying that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is the best framework for the Serb people, that there is a state there already, that there is the JNA which is the guarantor for the Serb people so that they could live in one state. If we Serbs do anything wrong, we would be the first to be blamed, so you insisted that we should be tolerant, that there was no need for arming, and that that simply could not be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me end on this note: Do you agree that it wasn't only that Prijedor tried to get out of Banja Luka's sphere of influence, but also has there not been this rivalry between Banja Luka and Sarajevo for decades regardless of who was in power? Did Banja Luka always want to be independent from Sarajevo just like Prijedor always wanted to be independent from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you mentioned Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Prijedor. Now, what did you actually mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me try to put it simply. Even way back from the times of socialism, is there -- is there this strong rivalry between Sarajevo and Banja Luka regardless of who's in power, Communists, Serbs, Muslims, whoever? Was there always this tendency in Banja Luka to be more independent from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was there during the times of the socialist system, and also it happened when the government had their seat in Sarajevo. And I know that full will that that is the case to this day because I work in Sarajevo and so I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1888, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Mr. Krejic, not only for your testimony, but I would also like to thank you for having carried out your duty in a way that can only be to your credit and to the credit of Republika Srpska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having stated that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland. How long will your re-examination take?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Hopefully not more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll do that now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, earlier today at pages 25 and 26, Mr. Karadzic asked you a question about -- "It seems to follow that the residents of Prijedor were rather independent even from Banja Luka, which was no more than 50 kilometres away." And you answered that you -- "Indeed, when we had meetings before the war and during the war, Chief Zupljanin held these meetings at the collegium attended by all the chiefs of the SJBs in the area of Banja Luka. And that at these meetings we gained a very clear impression. In fact, it was perfectly clear that he had next to no influence at all on the leading people from the SJB Prijedor --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down while reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "... and I mean first and foremost Simo Drljaca." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure your question was fully translated. Do you remember that part, Mr. Krejic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you remember the question and the answer that I just read to you, that -- that occurred earlier in today's proceeding?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I do remember. However, I don't think that it has been presented to me 100 per cent accurately. You said something like the residents of Prijedor being independent from Banja Luka. And I also don't think that I said -- I also did not say that Chief Zupljanin didn't have any influence whatsoever in Prijedor. I'm sure. You have confused me now, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. I will read again very slowly the question and the answer. The question was: "It seems to follow from that that the residents of Prijedor were rather independent even from Banja Luka, which was no more than 50 kilometres away." Your answer was: "I will limit my answer only to my line of work, that is to say public security. Indeed, when we had meetings before the war and during the war, Chief Zupljanin held these meetings at the collegium, attended by chiefs the public security centres in the area of Banja Luka and at these meetings we gained a very clear impression. In fact, it was perfectly clear that he had no next to no influence at all on the leading people from the public security station of Prijedor, and I mean, first and foremost, Simo Drljaca." And then you go on to say: "And other public security stations, Novi Grad and Bosanska Dubica."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? The interpretation said "residents of Prijedor," whereas I meant "policemen from Prijedor." It's probably my fault. I did not mean Prijedorcani, people of Prijedor in general terms. I meant Prijedorcani as in policemen from Prijedor. However, Mr. Krejic already corrected that through his answer because he restricted his answer to public security only.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you were then further -- you recall that question and answer?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I do recall that, and now you're question was more specific. Not only what Mr. Karadzic explained just now but also the first time I was told that I had said that the public security centre of Banja Luka and Chief Zupljanin did not have any influence whatsoever over the public security station in Prijedor; whereas, the second time you said it correctly, that they had a small influence only, and there is a distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, you -- or Mr. Karadzic then took you to an answer that you had given in the Ivankovic trial when he was referring to asking you questions about the second meeting with -- on the 30th of August, the one that General Subotic attended. And there in the transcript it says -- when he was quoting the transcript that you testified that: "That was the second time in my life that I saw Simo Drljaca. The first time I saw him was at that first meeting. But later I came to know him a little better." But how do you reconcile that with the answer here that you gave here that you -- indeed, when there were meetings before the war and during the war Zupljanin held these meetings at the collegium with all the SJBs, and then you go on to say that he had no influence over Prijedor, in particular, Drljaca? Or little -- next to no influence.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely. Just having meetings held does not mean that someone has influence over someone else. The fact that Chief Zupljanin held meetings does not mean that he held all the strings in his own hands, namely that the people from the public security station in Prijedor and primarily Chief Simo Drljaca listened to him and did his work in accordance with the law on regulations as one should.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said at transcript page 36 today that you only got to know Drljaca better in 1995/1996, and given that the first time you saw Drljaca was in late August 1992, therefore you had not met him before, during the earlier months, let's say between April and beginning of August, 1992. I just wanted to know how we are to reconcile the fact that you now say that Zupljanin had no influence over Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I would like to correct a mistake here, a mistake of my own. To err is human, so I should admit my own mistakes. During Ivankovic case, I think, or another case, I made a mistake. The lawyers put that question to me and I think that I made a mistake when I said that I first saw Simo at that first meeting in August, because it is a fact that I saw him before that as well, not many times. Perhaps two or three times. Not more than that. They drew my attention to that there and over there I did correct that. Now, before Simo Drljaca became chief, that is to say before the war, more frequent meeting were held, and at that time Simo Drljaca was not the chief in Prijedor. It was another man, a Muslim. I remember his first name was Hasan. I cannot remember his last name. That is to say that I admit that it was my mistake, but it is totally unintentional. When I said that I first met Simo on that first meeting on the 23rd in Banja Luka, it is possible --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the witnesses. Could all microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, the interpreters were not able to catch the last part of your answer when you said "it is possible."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite possible that I met Simo Drljaca some other time as well, not only during that first meeting that had to do with what had happened in Koricanske Stijene. That is my mistake, an unintentional mistake. That was indicated at the hearing in the court in Sarajevo, and I admitted that mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, what other time did you meet with Simo Drljaca between April and early August 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Up until the beginning of the war, the chief of the security services centre held meetings very often, joint meetings, with all the chiefs of the public security stations from the region. All the chiefs -- or, rather, out of the 16 of us, 14 were Serbs and two were Muslims, one from Prijedor and the other one from Jajce. When the war started, Simo Drljaca was appointed chief of the public security station in Prijedor, replacing this man whose first name was Hasan and whose last name I do not remember. When the war started, these meetings were held less frequently because of the crisis, because of the state of war. It is possible that from May until August I saw Simo Drljaca perhaps once or twice or three times maximum.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to take you now to another point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist with the last name of this man Hasan? I can just ask if it's the same Hasan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's necessary. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At page 32 of today's transcript, when we were discussing -- when you were discussing the second meeting on the 30th of August, 1992, where Minister Subotic attended, and -- and Mr. Karadzic put to you, and I'll read the question: "Thank you. You're right, and I'm in such a hurry. So as for the first questions put by Minister Subotic in terms of how come that happened, he tried to say that someone from the top leadership of the republic knew about that, and then he calmed down because he realized that Subotic was from the top leadership of the republic; right?" This was in relation to the earlier question put when Mr. Karadzic asked you when someone from the authorities -- when Drljaca tried to say that someone from the authorities would have to know about that. And in your -- your answer to Mr. Karadzic's question that I just put to you was: "Perhaps you could put it in that way. During my previous testimonies I never said, because no one asked me, what the response of -- was of Minister Subotic. Minister Subotic responded to Simo Drljaca that it was possible. I mean, when -- when Simo Drljaca said that the top leadership knew about that, Minister Subotic said that it was possible that orders, some kind of orders or instructions came regarding the freedom of movement, primarily the non-Serb population in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor and throughout Republika Srpska; whereas, Simo and the other top people from Prijedor abused that. They understood it in their own way. And this population transfer that they carried out was in contravention of the efforts made by the leadership of the republic. That is what Minister Subotic said briefly, and then Simo Drljaca had no comment or answer." Do you remember that question and answer from earlier today?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Your question is too long. I've lost the thread, and I'm not even sure when you are quoting me and when you are putting a question or making a suggestion. If you want me to answer properly, could you simplify the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, I read you word or word your answer. Do you recall -- and I'll read it again. This is what you said: "During my previous testimonies, I never said, because no one asked me, what the response was of Minister Subotic. Minister Subotic responded to Simo Drljaca that it was possible, I mean, when -- when Simo Drljaca said that the top leadership knew about that, Minister Subotic said that it -- it is possible that orders, some kind of orders or instructions came regarding the freedom of movement, primarily the non-Serb population in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor and throughout Republika Srpska; whereas, Simo and the other top people from Prijedor abused that." Do you recall saying that answer earlier today?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: That is better phrased now. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have -- I'm not sure of the 65 ter number. It's the Zecevic transcript in Mr. Krejic's testimony in the Zecevic case in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you have more than five minutes, we would better have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't wish to take more than five minutes. If we could go to page 17 in the English, and it's page 20 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that there's no English for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh. Your Honour, it -- I have -- I have an English translation here, so we do have it. I wonder if Mr. Reid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm afraid I've marked my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is a short passage --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's a short passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we can proceed --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I can possibly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- because the interpreter can see the B/C/S version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic -- Mr. Subotic. Mr. Krejic, do you recall saying this in the Zecevic case when you were asked by the Prosecutor about -- about this meeting, and then you said: "Well, Mr. Subotic went further than that. He first addressed Simo Drljaca directly by asking something to the effect of who allowed them to move the population from Prijedor at all, and that question was posed in a very stern form. I didn't know Simo very well but got to know him better later. This was the first time I saw him answer mildly. He was confused and didn't really have a proper answer, and finally Simo said, 'Why are you asking me this when you know better than I do who made the deal and how it was made?' Minister Subotic ignored that and asked for information." And your answer goes on. Do you recall stating that in the Zecevic trial?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember I stated that, but I added something that nobody had asked me, namely the answer of Minister Subotic, who said a few words precisely about that freedom of movement for the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned that today, that -- you said that nobody had asked you previously about what Mr. Subotic said after Simo Drljaca said, "Why are you asking me this when you know better than I do who made the deal and how it was made?" And today you said, "Well, nobody asked me before. Now I'm telling you what Mr. Subotic said, and he talked about the freedom of movement." I just read you a paragraph from the Zecevic trial where after exactly Simo said that, you testified under oath that Minister Subotic ignored that, and I'm just wondering how we reconcile those answers.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: He did not ask any further questions about the organisation of the movement of the population and convoys, et cetera. He only briefly mentioned some orders that the top leadership of Republika Srpska sent down to municipal authorities and lower-level authorities about the freedom of movement. It was not very articulate, but he did speak about that, and he didn't say much. He continued to talk mostly about Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And finally, you were taken to a number of documents involving the investigation and even documents showing involvement of the prosecutor in -- in the event which occurred at Koricanske Stijene on the 21st of August, 1992. Was anyone prosecuted for this crime to your knowledge between 1992 and 1995, the end of 1995, or at all before the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The answer to your question is already contained in one of the answers I have given to Mr. Karadzic earlier, namely that as of 1st September, I worked in a job that had nothing, but absolutely nothing to do with this case and cases like this, and I wasn't interested. I had a different kind of work. I was engaged in different assignments. And of course I heard a few things like any other resident of Banja Luka or Knezevo could at the time, but my job did nothing --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but your answer is either you know or you don't know whether anyone's been prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sutherland, I don't think you can put that observation in re-examination. You're trying to lead the witness into a limitation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I was simply asking if he knew to his knowledge whether anyone had been prosecuted, but I will -- I will leave it. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Thank you, Mr. Krejic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of my colleagues and the Tribunal I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague. Now you're free to go, but we'll rise all together. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00. Did you have anything, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed to hear the next witness, witness's evidence, there's an administrative matter to deal with in private session briefly. Shall the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, while we are bringing in the witness -- yes Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We received information that the Chamber would be sitting tomorrow morning to complete the testimony of this witness and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To accommodate the witness's request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and we don't have any problem with that, but I just wanted to let you know that I, myself, will not be available because of having to travel to Croatia and Bosnia, and I apologise for that but we'll be ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding and co-operation. In principle we will be sitting in Courtroom III tomorrow, but if there is a change, i.e., that there is not sitting for Haradinaj tomorrow, then we'll be sitting in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what time are we starting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 9.00. And I very much appreciate Mr. Harvey's understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness kindly make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Komljenovic. Would you make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Komljenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As we discussed, part of your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing. We first need to deal with the formalities in relation to that submission. You provided a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY on the 7th of December, 2009, and you also testified before the Bosnia and Herzegovina state court in the Prosecutor v. Ivankovic et al. Case on the 31st of March, 2009; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: A statement has been prepared which contains portions of your ICTY statement and your BiH testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If 65 ter number 90291 could be brought on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You recently had an opportunity to review this statement with the assistance of an interpreter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And during that review, paragraphs were -- we'll wait for the -- is -- in front of you on the computer screen is this the amalgamated witness statement - if we could scroll down the page - that you reviewed on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 1. The next page. Paragraphs 1 to 5 were read to you in a language you understood; correct? Because these -- if I -- if I may continue, because these paragraphs were taken from your ICTY statement from the 7th of December, 2009, and they were in the English language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please. Page 3 of the statement. And then, Mr. Komljenovic, with respect to paragraphs 6 to 24, that is the remainder of the statement, you reviewed these paragraphs by going through the B/C/S version, what is commonly referred to as B/C/S version, that is the -- the Serbian version of your BiH testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to the first five paragraphs which were read back to you, you wished to make two clarifications and two corrections in paragraph 4. The two clarifications are contained in footnote 6 and 7, and that was in relation to meetings and also in relation to a dispatch, and then the two corrections that you wish to make, also in paragraph 4, related to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Well, the two corrections are on this page, Your Honour, page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The two corrections that you wish to make related to the word "conclusion" and also in relation to "make accessible," which was in relation to the bodies from the massacre; is that correct? And -- and that is contained in footnotes 7 and 8, the two corrections.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The correction refers to the term "remove." I had an objection, because the term was not used at the meeting. It was about allowing access to the bodies of the dead persons. That's one thing, and we agree that term should be changed and also that the term "order" should be replaced by "conclusions," because it was more conclusions than an order by Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Then also during the review, there were two matters which were found to be incorrect in the English translation, and that was in relation to paragraph 7. The word as it stands now -- it's the fifth line from the bottom of paragraph 7, which is on page 5 of the statement. The sentence reads: "So it is possible that --" It currently reads in this version in front of you: "So it is possible that the local chief knew, had the information, but I did not have the information." And the word "police" should be inserted between "local" and "chief"; is that right? So it's the "local police chief"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 9, the fifth line, the word "mobilised" was to be corrected, and this is simply -- I'll read the -- the -- the answer that you gave in the -- the state court: "Yes, of course. I found out about the event that took place on the 21st, that was simply an event which had its impact and we were all mobilised when that happened." And the word "mobilised" should be "got up on our feet." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not really an adequate term. I -- I believe that your version "to get up on our feet" was better. We were all in a state of shock, but we were not mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct. And the interpreter that was reviewing this statement with you went back to the B/C/S version of your transcript and found that, in fact, you had said "got up on our feet." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the interpretation in such great detail, but, yes, that could be an adequate expression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, I just wanted to take you to paragraph 12. It's on page 9, and it was dealing with -- paragraph 12 was dealing with whose area of responsibility it was, who -- and -- and you said it was the area of responsibility of the 22nd Brigade. And then you mention a colonel, and in the -- in the B/C/S transcript, the Bosnian transcript. And this is 65 ter number 22145. At page 66 of that transcript, it actually spells Mr. Peulic's name Peuvic, P-e-u-v-i-c in the transcript, but in fact - correct me if I am wrong - you're actually referring to Colonel Peulic there at that point.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in paragraph 13, this is on page 10 of your amalgamated statement, when you were talking about the meeting on the 13th of August, and this is the fifth line down, you were mentioning some names of people who were there, and in the Bosnian transcript it actually says "Djuro Gulic," and again correct me if I am wrong, it's supposed -- it was supposed to read "Djuro Bulic"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Djuro Bulic is the name, Djuro Bulic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Komljenovic, you then signed the amalgamated statement. Can you confirm to the Court today that the amalgamated statement with your clarifications and corrections accurately reflects your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, in -- in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were asked today about the matters contained in your amalgamated statement, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't change anything. More or less this is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's -- if you couldn't formulate everything in exactly the same words, what you're saying is the essence would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously things could be worded differently. Things could be interpreted differently, but in essence, my statement would still remain the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter number 90291.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3768, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with Your Honours' leave I'll now read a summary of the witness's written evidence. Mr. Komljenovic is of Serb ethnicity. In 1992, he was the president of the Skender Vakuf Municipal Assembly and president of the Skender Vakuf Crisis Staff. The Skender Vakuf municipality changed its name to the Knezevo municipality. The witness described convoys of non-Serb inhabitants from municipalities within the Autonomous Region of Krajina, including Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Prijedor, being transported through the Skender Vakuf/Knezevo municipality towards Travnik in the summer of 1992. He testified -- he describes the aftermath of the Koricanske Stijene massacre on the 21st of August, 1992, which is Schedule B, 15.6. On the 22nd of August, 1992, the witness learned of the massacre at Koricanske Stijene and immediately went to the site. He described what he saw as a "picture of horror." The witness looked down into the abyss and saw bunches of people, one over the other, hanging from the branches and rocks. The witness estimated that the number of bodies could be around 200. He returned to Skender Vakuf/Knezevo and attempted to contact Stojan Zupljanin to report the massacre. He was unable to reach Stojan Zupljanin on the phone or in person in Banja Luka. Mr. Komljenovic then travelled to Prijedor to see Milomir Stakic. The witness demanded that Stakic and the Prijedor authorities remove the bodies -- or make the bodies accessible, I should say better, because Prijedor police had committed the crime. The witness testified that it was a common knowledge that the victims of the massacre were Muslims from Prijedor and that the massacre was committed by people from Prijedor who escorted the convoy. Shortly thereafter the witness travelled to Banja Luka with Nenad Krejic and Vladimir Glamocic for a meeting with Stojan Zupljanin, Milomir Stakic, and Simo Drljaca from Prijedor, and others also, in relation to the recovery of the bodies of the massacre. The witness states that Stojan Zupljanin discussed with him a dispatch from Radovan Karadzic. The witness stated that possibly after the first meeting, the civilian protection unit from Skender Vakuf/Knezevo removed four bodies and buried them above the road. In addition, the witness provides evidence in relation to a meeting held in Banja Luka on the 30th of August, 1992, which was chaired by Republika Srpska minister of defence, Bogdan Subotic. The meeting was attended by RS MUP personnel and civilian authorities from Banja Luka, Prijedor, and Skender Vakuf/Knezevo. The witness and Vlado Glamocic made notes on the conclusions from this meeting. One of the conclusions was that the Prijedor authorities were to clear the terrain and make the bodies from the ravine accessible in order to allow for further processing of the case. The witness states that after the Prijedor authorities were tasked with the removal of the bodies from the massacre, the Skender Vakuf/Knezevo representatives were excluded from participation in the further developments and received no official information. Unofficially, the witness received information that people from Prijedor had a crane and brought some equipment from Prijedor mines but that the crane broke down and they could not complete the job. The witness stated that there were rumours that the bodies, the remaining bodies, were -- were burnt or explosives were put into the abyss. The witness also stated that three or four months prior to December 2009, Vlado Glamocic admitted to him that on the night of the massacre, Glamocic received an enraged telephone call from Radovan Karadzic demanding answers about the massacre and who was responsible for it. Your Honour, that completes the summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, I have a few questions for you. You have stated in your amalgamated statement that you tried to contact Stojan Zupljanin and went to Banja Luka but couldn't find him, and then you went to Prijedor to see Milomir Stakic. What did Stakic say to you when you -- when you confronted him about this event that had happened in Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously we had a problem after this event. Things came to a head between us and Prijedor. Knezevo as a local commune could not take all the necessary measures, primarily works within the competence of the civilian protection. We wanted the municipality of Prijedor to get involved, because those were their fellow citizens. The relations came to a head during the first meeting, and then during the second meeting I asked Stakic to help us get the bodies out of the gorge, that they should be made accessible to investigating bodies and for the bodies to be returned to Prijedor and buried there because they were citizens of Prijedor. I didn't -- he didn't really appreciate what I'd said, and the problem came to a head at the meeting on the 3rd -- 30th of August. The citizens of Prijedor refused to get involved and refused to lend a hand in removing the bodies and helping the other bodies to do their work. And you will find that in the minutes of the records -- of the meetings where it says that the bodies should be approached, they should be taken out from that place, they should be made available to the investigating bodies who should then do their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we will get --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly sit closer to the microphones, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're being asked if you can come closer to the microphones. The interpreters are having difficulty hearing you. Or if you can speak up a little. We'll get to the 30th of August meeting in one moment, but do you recall going to a meeting with Mr. Krejic and Mr. Glamocic with -- with Mr. Zupljanin in Banja Luka before you have the meeting with -- that's -- with Mr. Subotic on the 30th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned that in your amalgamated statement that a dispatch from Mr. Karadzic was discussed informally between Mr. Zupljanin and yourself. What -- what was discussed between you at that informal meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin mentioned some dispatch in the sense that both municipalities should take necessary measures to do the work that should be done after a massacre had been committed. Of course, I did not see the dispatch myself but Mr. Zupljanin told me what the dispatch said. The essence was that the two municipalities stop quarreling and that at that moment they try to recover the bodies so the appropriate organs could do their own work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Moving on to the 30th of August meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 13299 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, do you recognise what's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: It is my diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 19 of the B/C/S and page 13 of the English. Sorry, page 20 of the B/C/S. It's actually page 19 in the version that I have in -- in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you take that to Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, yes. 0637783. Thank you very much, Your Honour. And if we could just go to the previous page in English. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, do we see on the -- in front of us the page of your diary which has the notes of the meeting that was held in Banja Luka on the 30th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer. The interpreters didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you said this is your notebook. Is this your handwriting here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Not on the first page but on the second one on the right-hand side, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Since I and the president of the Executive Board sat next to each other, he wrote this note. He kept the minutes. This is the very clear handwriting in the Latin script, whereas this totally illegible scroll on the right-hand side is my own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can go to the next page of the B/C/S. That's -- and this is ERN 06397784. Is that a continuation of the meeting and that is your notes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are my notes. I would say the left-hand side of this side, if I can put it that way. I'm not sure about what it says here on the right, "Judge Maric, president of the court Maric," because we had not recorded him as attending the meeting, so I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page for English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can go back to the next page in both. You mentioned earlier that -- that in the meeting it was -- it was explained. One of the conclusions was that the bodies had to be made accessible for further -- for further things to -- to be done in relation to the bodies. Who was involved? What -- sorry, I'll start again. What involvement did the Skender Vakuf/Knezevo people -- what role do they have in doing this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the first meeting with regard to a few details only. Basically the first meeting failed, and that is why this other meeting that we're talking about now took place. It failed because the people of Prijedor did not want to take part. They did not want to help work on the bodies. Mr. Zupljanin tried to persuade them, and in fact he was between a rock and a hard place, between us and them. They were trying to get out of this, and it was probably Colonel Subotic who called this meeting in order to influence the Prijedor men to take part of the responsibility to get the bodies out, because nobody was doing anything. And the civilian protection of Knezevo, in view of the men who were there, they were old, weak, ill-equipped, and they were simply not in a position to do it, also in view of the landscape involved. So this meeting is a result of the failure of the previous meeting, and the essence of this meeting was that the Prijedor men should take part in this, as they had refused to do beforehand, that they should take it upon themselves to get the bodies out so that the organs would be in a position to identify the bodies, or, rather, to do all the work that was required in such situations in accordance with the law. So that is the essence; one, for Prijedor to take this responsibility because we were not in a position to do so; and the second point is that the work should be done as the diary says. It says quite clearly here that the operation would be led by Simo Drljaca and that our duty was this scribbling of mine shows that, that we provide them with food and a place to sleep, although that did not happen either. We didn't participate even from that point of view. And also that they should come with men and equipment, including firefighters so that this could be done properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we go back to -- and that's -- you've referred to that as being on the left-hand side of that text, on the left-hand side of your illegible -- with your illegible handwriting. If we go back to the page before where it has the participants of the meeting, and then we see on the right-hand side page there it says: "Identification at the site," how many corpses are to be identified, and then "CZ," which is the civilian protection of the municipality where it happened. And then I think you've also written in your handwriting, "Engage the CZ," the civilian protection. What was that in relation to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the conclusions. Most of them are on the left-hand side as written by Glamocic, and they say to provide for identification on the scene itself, and the second one is actually a question: "How many corpses are to be identified?" That is what was discussed, since access to the bodies was a major problem. So the question was how many corpses could be retrieved in the first place during the course of one day. And then involve the civilian protection. We had already involved the civilian protection. We tried to get a few bodies out. You mentioned that already, that the civilian protection of Knezevo retrieved four bodies and buried them above the road. Later on they were exhumed, and I don't know what happened then. And then, of course, pathologists, pathologists should get involved too. That's what it says at the end. The essence of these conclusions was that everything should be done as should invariably be done in such cases so that the appropriate authorities could deal with that, and I repeat once again so that what is in accordance with the law could be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was the head of the civilian protection in Skender Vakuf/Knezevo municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: At the time we had a Council for National Defence, or, rather, we had a Secretariat of National Defence that was still functioning. The secretary of the secretariat was, in fact, the head of the civilian protection, and they had a company of their own, and the commander of this company was Cedo Vukovic, and the secretary of the secretariat was Ostoja Barisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was Cedo Vukovic about the place or did he have to be brought back from somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: We intervened through the military to have Cedo returned because he was in a military unit. We asked for him to be returned and to take over the civilian protection unit, and that is indeed what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So he was part of a military unit at the front?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the time. Do you have more?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was about to say thank you, Mr. Komljenovic. That's all the questions that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We should have risen a minute ago, but I have to continue a bit --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering only those two pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3769, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we have decided to sit tomorrow in order to accommodate the witness's request. We are always trying to -- to accommodate them, but I'm very reluctant to ask you, but whether you can finish your cross-examination in less than two hours' time tomorrow. The maximum amount of time that we can sit for tomorrow is two hours with -- i.e., two one-hour session with a 15-minute break. Otherwise, we'll just cancel tomorrow's sitting and we'll continue next week.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, it all depends on the witness, on Mr. Komljenovic. If he really has to be brought back next week, then I will do my best tomorrow to finish on time, because it would be a pity, though. Mr. Komljenovic is also a political figure, he is familiar with the process of the creation of the community of municipalities. He took part in political life, so it would be useful for the Trial Chamber to hear from him about all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But -- yes. Mr. Komljenovic, my understanding is that if required and if necessary, you can stay till next week. Is my understanding correct, Mr. Komljenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am ready to accommodate Mr. Karadzic and stay, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, I don't see the point of sitting tomorrow at the sacrifice of having the benefit of presence of Judge Lattanzi as well as Mr. Robinson. So we will adjourn for this week, and I will resume next week on Tuesday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is Your Honour going to warn Mr. Komljenovic that he can't discuss his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Probably you will be aware already that you are not supposed to discuss about your evidence with anybody else outside the courtroom. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate very much your kind understanding. Please have a nice weekend. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is also grateful. The Defence is also grateful to the witness for the effort he has made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of November, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.
